title: Restoring the air
teaches: That plants make oxygen only in light but breathe all the time, and how a leaf's balance sets where it can live

blocks.text: Joseph Priestley was a dissenting minister in Leeds, in the north of England, who did chemistry in his spare time. He lived next door to a brewery, and he got interested in the gas that rose off the fermenting vats, the gas van Helmont had found in burning charcoal and called gas sylvestre, which chemists of Priestley's day called “fixed air”: carbon dioxide. Before long he was collecting and testing every kind of “air” he could make.

Everyone knew that a candle burning in a closed jar soon goes out, and that a mouse sealed in a jar soon dies. The air was “injured” somehow, and stayed injured. On 17 August 1771 Priestley put a sprig of mint into a jar of air in which a wax candle had burned out, standing it in a little water, and left it. On the 27th he lowered another candle into the jar, and it burned perfectly well. The mint had restored the air.

He tried other plants, and they did it too. In 1772 he reported that a mouse could live in air that a plant had restored. He thought he had found how the world's air, constantly fouled by fires, breathing and rot, was kept fit to breathe. “The injury which is continually done to the atmosphere by the respiration of such a large number of animals,” he wrote, “… is, in part at least, repaired by the vegetable creation.”

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Priestley (1771) found a sprig of mint, in ten days, restored air in which a candle had burned out.
He thought plants keep the world's air fit to breathe.

blocks.text: Then it stopped working. When Priestley and others tried again, sometimes the plants restored the air and sometimes they made it worse. Priestley himself began to doubt his own result. A finding that comes and goes is worse than useless: either there is no effect, or there is something you're not controlling.

Jan Ingenhousz found what it was. He was a Dutch-born doctor, famous for inoculating the Austrian imperial family against smallpox, and in the summer of 1779 he rented a house at Southall, outside London, and ran more than five hundred experiments in three months. He put leaves under water in glass jars and watched for bubbles of gas, collecting them and measuring how good the gas was with a test Priestley had invented.

His answer was light. Leaves in sunshine gave off bubbles of good air within hours. The same leaves in shade, or at night, gave off none, and the air around them got worse. Only the green parts did it: roots, flowers and fruit made the air worse in light or dark. Priestley's failures had been plants kept in dim rooms. Ingenhousz published the same year, in a book whose title says it all: *Experiments upon Vegetables, Discovering Their Great Power of Purifying the Common Air in the Sun-shine, and of Injuring It in the Shade and at Night*. The good air was what the French chemist Antoine Lavoisier was just then naming **oxygen**.

blocks.caption: Priestley's jar of spent air with a sprig of mint, sealed, in daylight or kept dark. A model.
blocks.task: Guess, then run ten days in the light and ten in the dark

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Ingenhousz (1779) found plants restore the air only in light, and only their green parts.
In the shade and at night, plants make the air worse.

blocks.text: What Ingenhousz saw is two processes running in the same leaf. One is photosynthesis, from lesson 1: in light, green cells take in carbon dioxide and water and make sugar, giving off oxygen. The other is **respiration**, which is how every living cell gets energy to work: it burns sugar with oxygen, slowly and under control, and gives off carbon dioxide and water. It is the same reaction as the log burning in the fireplace, run in tiny steps so that the energy is caught instead of lost as flame.

Animals only respire. Plants do both. Their roots, flowers, stems and fruit respire all the time, and so do their leaves, day and night. In the dark, respiration is all that happens, and a plant behaves like a small, slow animal. In daylight, photosynthesis in the leaves usually runs many times faster than respiration, so the plant as a whole takes in carbon dioxide and gives off oxygen. What we see is the difference between the two.

A common mix-up is that plants photosynthesise *instead* of breathing. They don't. A potato in a cupboard, with no green parts and no light, is respiring the whole time it sits there, slowly using up its own starch. That is why stored potatoes get lighter and why a sack of grain stored damp gets warm.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: **Respiration** burns sugar with oxygen to release energy; every living cell does it, all the time.
Plants respire and photosynthesise; what we see is the difference between the two.
In the dark a plant only respires, like an animal.

blocks.text: Because a leaf is always respiring, it gains only when light is bright enough for photosynthesis to outrun respiration. As the light fades, there is a level where the two exactly balance: the leaf makes as much sugar as it burns. Below it, the leaf is a cost to the plant. Above it, the leaf pays its way.

blocks.caption: Sugar gained by a sun leaf and a shade leaf of the same tree, as the light changes. On this scale full summer sun is about 2,000. A model with the shapes measured for real leaves.
blocks.task: Find a light where the shade leaf gains and the sun leaf loses

blocks.text: A tree solves this by building two kinds of leaf. Leaves at the top of the crown, in full sun, are thick, with several layers of cells packed with the machinery of photosynthesis. In bright light they make a great deal of sugar. But all that machinery costs a lot to keep running, so they respire a lot, and they break even only in fairly good light. Leaves deep in the crown are thin and broad with less machinery. They can never make as much, but they cost so little to run that they break even in dim light that would starve a sun leaf.

The light on a forest floor can be only one or two percent of the light above the canopy. Plants that live there, such as ferns, mosses and the seedlings of shade-tolerant trees, have leaves built cheap. It is one of the main reasons some trees can grow up in a forest's shade and others can't, which matters a great deal when a forest regrows after a fire or a felling.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: A leaf gains only above the light at which photosynthesis balances respiration.
Sun leaves make much more in bright light but cost more to run; shade leaves break even in dimmer light.
On a forest floor only cheap, shade-built leaves can pay their way.

blocks.text: Ingenhousz didn't know what plants did with the “fixed air” they took in. In 1782 the Swiss pastor Jean Senebier showed that leaves give off good air only if the water contains dissolved carbon dioxide, and in 1804 his countryman Nicolas-Théodore de Saussure weighed plants and the gases around them very carefully. The carbon a plant gains, he showed, comes from the carbon dioxide it takes in. And the plant gains more weight than that carbon alone, because it builds water into itself too. Van Helmont's willow was finally explained.

Priestley's hope was right on the largest scale. Nearly all the oxygen in the air was put there by photosynthesis, over billions of years, and nearly all the carbon dioxide that animals, fires and rot give off is taken back up by plants and algae. But the balance is a balance: by day, by night, and through the seasons, the world's plants both breathe in and breathe out.

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Senebier (1782) showed leaves need carbon dioxide to make oxygen; de Saussure (1804) showed plants build their mass from carbon dioxide and water.
Nearly all the oxygen in the air was made by photosynthesis.

blocks.caption: Six questions on light and breath
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: A sealed jar holds a mouse and a potted plant. It's kept dark for a day. What happens to the oxygen?
choices: It falls: both the mouse and the plant use it
It stays level: the plant replaces what the mouse uses
items.why: In the dark the plant only respires, using oxygen just as the mouse does.

items.ask: Why did Priestley's experiment sometimes fail when people repeated it?
choices: The plants weren't getting enough light
The mint was the wrong kind
items.why: Ingenhousz showed that plants restore the air only in light. In dim rooms, respiration wins.

items.ask: Which parts of a plant respire?
choices: Every living part, all the time
items.why: Respiration is how every living cell gets energy. Leaves, roots, stems, flowers and fruit all do it, day and night.

items.ask: A thick sun leaf and a thin shade leaf are put in dim light. Which is more likely to gain sugar?
items.why: The shade leaf respires much less, so it breaks even at a lower light. The sun leaf's costly machinery outruns what it can make in dim light.

items.ask: On a bright day a leaf gives off oxygen. What is happening inside it?
choices: Photosynthesis is running faster than respiration
items.why: Both run at once. We see the difference: in bright light photosynthesis wins by a wide margin.

items.ask: Potatoes stored in a dark cupboard slowly get lighter. Why?
choices: They respire, burning their own starch
items.why: A potato is living tissue. With no light it can only respire, using up its stored starch and giving off carbon dioxide and water.

summary: **Priestley (1771): a sprig of mint restored air in which a candle had burned out.**
**Ingenhousz (1779): only in light, and only the green parts.** In the shade and at night plants make the air worse.
**Plants photosynthesise and respire.** Respiration burns sugar with oxygen; every living cell does it all the time.
**What we see is the difference.** In bright light photosynthesis wins; in the dark a plant only respires.
**A leaf pays its way only above the light where the two balance.**
**Sun leaves make more in bright light but cost more; shade leaves break even in dim light.** Forest-floor plants need cheap leaves.
**Senebier and de Saussure finished the story.** Plants build themselves from carbon dioxide and water, and nearly all the air's oxygen was made by photosynthesis.
